6: 1. "Settings" sheet: start with the production kitchen staff block. The production kitchen's cost per hour is NOT an industry figure and you don't type it: it's calculated from the base pay in your wage table, the pay periods, each person's FTE and the payroll taxes, workers' comp and benefits the employer pays. Below that are the purchase prices, one per ingredient: it's the only table where prices are entered, and all 226 lines of the recipe costing draw from it.
7: 2. "Batch Costing" sheet: one row per ingredient and per item. The costing unit is THE BATCH, not the piece: that's how a production kitchen works, and it's the only way labor adds up. Enter the net quantity you use, the factor that converts the purchase unit into the unit of use (12 to go from a dozen to each, 1 if they match) and the trim loss. The line cost calculates itself.
8: 3. "Labor Cost per Hour" sheet: the minutes each batch takes and the selling price. From there come labor cost per piece, total cost, food cost and margin in dollars. It's the sheet that teaches you to stop giving your work away.
9: 4. "Egg & TCS Decision" sheet: for each item, choose the egg route and say whether it's filled and whether the finished item is shelf-stable at room temperature. The workbook returns the holding temperature, which test applies and whether the item needs a date mark when held more than 24 hours. The shelf life is yours to declare.
10: 5. "Mix and Average Ticket" sheet: split 100% of your units across the 30 items. That gives you your average ticket, which you can't copy from a study because we found no reliable published average ticket for bakeries.
11: 6. "Menu Decision" sheet: it crosses margin with turnover and tells you what to keep, what to review the price of and what to drop. Go over it three months after opening, with real sales, and again each time the season changes.

13: What to know before you start
14: THE MARGIN RULE IS ONE RULE, SAID TWO WAYS. A 65-70% gross margin and a 30-35% food cost are the same number seen from either side: if food cost is 32%, gross margin is 68%. That's why "Settings" asks you for ONE and calculates the other. Any tool that asks for both will let you enter them inconsistently.
15: THERE'S NO "TWO TEMPERATURES" CONFLICT. The sheet runs two checks (filled and not shelf-stable; an egg route that leaves the item needing cold) and both lead to the same Food Code limit: 41 °F or below (3-501.16). And the part almost nobody keeps track of: ready-to-eat TCS food held more than 24 hours has to be date marked, 7 days at most, with the day you make it counting as day 1 (3-501.17).
16: THIS WORKBOOK DOESN'T CALCULATE SHELF LIFE, AND NO WORKBOOK CAN. The Food Code doesn't set it: you do, with your process and your tests, and it goes in your food safety plan. What the sheet does carry is the legal ceiling, the date mark, which is a different thing and has its own column.
17: WHERE THE ALLERGENS ARE, BECAUSE THEY'RE NOT HERE. The display-case allergen matrix (the written notice of the 9 major food allergens in unpackaged food, Food Code 3-602.12(C)) lives in the HACCP Food Safety Kit Pro. This workbook doesn't repeat it: never two full allergen declarations of the same menu in two files.
18: THE DAILY TEMPERATURES AREN'T HERE EITHER. Temperature logs are in the HACCP Food Safety Kit Pro. What this workbook makes is the decision that comes BEFORE: which egg route you choose for each item and what holding temperature that choice brings with it.
19: UNIT COSTING AND THE METHOD. If you want the unit costing of three pastry preparations, that's the Food Cost Kit Pro (05-bakery-cake-pricing); if you want the batch costing method and menu engineering, that's the Food Cost + Menu Engineering Guide. The 70% dark chocolate cake, the croissants and the macarons carry the SAME costing here as in the kit: copied and declared, never linked. A customer who owns both products can't see two different costs for the same croissant.
20: THE FOOD COST IN THE RECIPE COSTING AND THE ONE IN THE FINANCIAL PLAN DON'T MATCH, AND THAT'S FINE. The piece's food cost counts only ingredients. The one that reaches the P&L adds real waste, packaging, the third-party products the front counter resells and ingredient price increases. The "Mix and Average Ticket" sheet calculates both and shows the gap: that's your cushion, not an error.
21: THE EXAMPLE PURCHASE PRICES BELONG TO A MODELED KITCHEN. Nineteen are copied exactly from the Food Cost Kit Pro; the rest are plausible assumptions for professional purchasing, not US quotes. Delete them and enter your own invoices: a recipe costing built on someone else's prices is worth nothing.
22: How often you use this workbook: purchase prices EVERY TIME a supplier raises a price, and at least once a quarter. The recipe costing and the labor minutes, when you build the menu and every time you change a process. The egg and temperature decision, ONCE per item and every time you add a new one: it decides how many feet of refrigerated case you need. The mix, the average ticket and the menu decision, three months after opening and then every season.
23: To edit the structure or a cell that isn't green, unprotect the sheet: Review > Unprotect Sheet. The protection has NO password; it only stops you from overwriting a formula by accident.

88: This is the ONLY margin number you type. 365: HOW TO READ THIS SHEET. You choose the egg route and say whether the piece is filled and whether the FINISHED item is shelf-stable at room temperature. With that, the workbook gives you the temperature you have to hold it at, which test applies and whether it needs a date mark when held more than 24 hours. Nothing more, and nothing less.
366: SHELF LIFE IS YOURS. Column L reads "Declare in your food safety plan" on purpose: the Food Code does NOT set shelf lives, and this workbook won't invent them for your 30 items. You set them with your process and your tests, and they go in your food safety plan. The date mark in column K is a different thing: it's a legal ceiling (held more than 24 hours, 7 days at most) and it only covers ready-to-eat TCS food.
367: WHAT THIS SHEET CHANGES IN YOUR MONEY. Every item that comes out "Refrigerated case" is feet of refrigerated case you have to buy, and every item with a date mark is product on a clock: past 24 hours it needs a date mark, and 7 days is the most it can be held. That's why you read this sheet BEFORE you close the menu and BEFORE you buy the display case.
368: WHERE THE REST IS. The display-case allergen matrix and the daily temperature log are in the HACCP Food Safety Kit Pro. This workbook doesn't redo them: it makes the decision that comes before.
369: CHECK YOUR STATE'S EDITION. Your inspector enforces your state's adopted edition of the Food Code, not necessarily the 2022 model; the 2022 rules are the direction of travel, so building to them is the safe choice. Every cell with a legal figure on this sheet carries a note with the section and the link, checked in October 2026.
370: WHAT THIS SHEET DOESN'T COVER, AND WHY. Cooling and freezing belong to the PROCESS, not the display case: they go in your food safety plan and your temperature logs (cooling: Food Code 3-501.14). The 9 major food allergens have their own dedicated matrix in the HACCP Food Safety Kit Pro: repeating them in this table would mean keeping the same data in two places until they drift apart. And anything you package in the shop ahead of time, like bagged bread, needs a full label (3-602.11(B)), which chapter 3 of the guide covers.

405: WHY THE MENU FOOD COST AND THE ONE IN THE FINANCIAL PLAN DON'T MATCH. The recipe costing counts only the ingredients of what you make. The one that reaches the P&L adds four things, in this order of size: THIRD-PARTY products the front counter resells (drinks, coffee, ice cream, bought-in chocolates), which have no costing of their own; real waste, which in fresh product runs above target; packaging; and ingredient price increases, which in butter and cocoa aren't theoretical. That's why the financial plan is projected with the industry rule and not with your recipe costing: it's the conservative assumption. The gap between the two numbers is your cushion.
406: THE MIX IS MEASURED, NOT GUESSED. The one in the example is an assumption. Yours comes out of your POS in two clicks three months after opening, and until then any average ticket you calculate is a hypothesis. Say so when you take it to the bank.

421: Within target and turning over: it's an item that holds up the menu. Watch that its ingredient cost doesn't get away from you.

429: HOW IT'S DECIDED. Two questions, not four. Is the food cost within your target? Does the item turn over above your threshold? If the margin fails and it doesn't turn over either, it's out. If only the margin fails, the problem is price or process, not the menu: dropping it would cost you turnover. If neither fails, it stays.
430: THIS ISN'T MENU ENGINEERING. Menu engineering (Kasavana-Smith, Miller, Pavesic, Goal Value) is in the Food Cost + Menu Engineering Guide, with its four methods and how they compare. This is the menu traffic light for an OPENING menu, which is something else: you use it before you've sold anything, with the mix YOU assume.
431: WHEN TO LOOK AGAIN. Three months after opening, with real POS sales in the mix column, and then every time the season changes. An opening menu that's unchanged after a year is a menu nobody has looked at.
432: AN ITEM CAN STAY EVEN IF IT LOSES MONEY, AND YOU NEED TO KNOW IT. The baguette is the classic case: thin margin and lots of turnover, but it's what brings the customer in every day. If you decide to keep something the menu traffic light says to drop, write it down and set a date to review it: that's a decision, not an oversight.
